blocks.text: But there is also one species of the common lizard that is ἀμμώδης [ammōdēs]. Damir, in the chapter العظاة [al-ʿaẓāh] Aladha, or On the Lizard: وهي انواع كثيرة منها الابيض والاحمر والاصغر وكلها منقطه بالسواد والوان بحسب مساكنها فان منها ما يسكن الرمال ومنها ما يسكن قريبا من الما والعشب [wa-hiya anwāʿ kathīra minhā al-abyaḍ wa-al-aḥmar wa-al-aṣghar wa-kulluhā munaqqaṭa bi-al-sawād wa-alwān bi-ḥasab masākinihā fa-inna minhā mā yaskun al-rimāl wa-minhā mā yaskun qarīban min al-mā wa-al-ʿushb] There are many species of them: some white, some red, some yellow; all of them are spotted with black. And their colours correspond to the place they occupy. For some live in the sands, others near waters and in grassy places. And Alazhari: هي دويبة ملسا تعدوا وتترد كثيرا تشبه سام ابرص الا انها احسن منه وتسي العظاه وشحمة الارض وشحمة الرمل [hiya duwaybba malsā taʿdū wa-tataraddad kathīran tushbih sāmm abraṣ illā annahā aḥsan minhu wa-tusī al-ʿaẓāh wa-shaḥmat al-arḍ wa-shaḥmat al-raml] It is a soft animal, running about a great deal and going back and forth, similar to the sammabras, or stellio, except that it is prettier than it. It is called aladha, and Fat of the earth, and fat of the sand. You see, reader, that both this lizard and the other, less common one discussed above take their name from sand, just as the Hebrew חומט chomet does. Therefore חומט chomet signifies either one of the two, or both ^{(2)}.

Note in passing that عظاية [ʿaẓāya] or عضاية [ʿaḍāya] is used in Avicenna for the salamander, and in Abenbitar sometimes for the salamander, sometimes for the seps or Chalcidian lizard, not without serious error. For both of these are venomous. But العظاة [al-ʿaẓāh] lacks venom, as the Arabs explicitly teach. Damir: ومن خرافات العرب قالوا ان السوم لما فرق علي الحيوان احتبست العظاة [II, 503] عند التفرقة حتي نفد السم واخذ كل حيوان قسطه منه علي قدر السبق اليه فلم يكن لها فيه نصيب وفي طبعها انها عتشي مشيا سريعا ثم تقف ويقال [col. 1078] ان ذلك يعرض لها من التذكرة والاسف علي ما فاتها من السم [wa-min khurāfāt al-ʿArab qālū anna al-sūm lammā furriqa ʿalā al-ḥayawān iḥtabasat al-ʿaẓāh ʿinda al-tafriqa ḥattā nafida al-summ wa-akhadha kull ḥayawān qisṭahu minhu ʿalā qadr al-sabq ilayhi fa-lam yakun lahā fīhi naṣīb wa-fī ṭabʿihā annahā ʿatmshī mashyan sarīʿan thumma taqif wa-yuqāl anna dhālika yaʿriḍ lahā min al-tadhkira wa-al-asaf ʿalā mā fātahā min al-summ] It is one of the fables of the Arabs that they say that, when venoms were distributed among the animals, the aladha held back while the distribution was taking place, until the venoms ran out, each animal having taken its portion according to the order in which it had come first. And it got no portion. Accordingly, since it is natural to it to move at a rapid pace and then suddenly stop, they say this happens to it because it remembers and grieves that venom was denied it. In the same place Damir: وتمسي بارض مصر السحلية [wa-tumsī bi-arḍ Miṣr al-suḥliyya] In the land of Egypt it is called SUCHLIA, which Azhari asserts is similar to the stellio, الا انها لا تودي وهي احسن منه [illā annahā lā tūdī wa-hiya aḥsan minhu] except that it is not harmful, and is prettier than it. Those, therefore, must be mistaken who confuse this little animal with the salamander or with the Chalcidian lizard, which are extremely harmful.
